newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian president's major political backer killed.
newsitem.headline: Algerian president's major political backer killed.

text.p: In a defiant challenge to Algerian President Liamine Zeroual, gunmen shot dead one of his main political backers, trade union chief Abdelhak Benhamouda.

Hours after Benhamouda was assassinated on Tuesday, a booby-trapped parcel exploded in the garrison town of Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of the capital Algiers, killing one person and wounding 17, the Algerian security forces said.
Algeria's main military and paramilitary headquarters are located in the town.
The government said Moslem fundamentalists killed Benhamouda, the best known figure to die in over two weeks of intensified bloodshed which has marked the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
Zeroual, who only four days earlier had vowed to eradicate "terrorism" from Algeria, mourned Benhamouda's death as a loss for the country and its workers.
Four gunmen lay in wait for Benhamouda, head of the million-member Union Generale des Travailleurs Algeriens (UGTA), and shot him as he left union headquarters.
An Algerian opposition group, claiming to be supported by hundreds of thousands of people, urged Algerians to reject what it called both government repression and the ruthless guerrilla campaign.

"Now, there is no political force able to impose peace. Only the people can do so. This is why we call on the people... asking them to refuse to be hostage of one camp or the other. They must speak out against the violence," said the group named the Signatories of the Peace Call.

Zeroual told the country last Friday that legal opposition leaders were hiding behind "the calls for peace... calls whose sole truth lies in an invitation to the Algerian people to resign themselves to assassination, destruction and hegemony".
Just hours before Benhamouda was shot, an Italian Foreign Ministry official said Rome would propose a peace initiative at a meeting next week with France and Spain.
In France, trade unions condemned the killing.
At least 176 people have been killed since January 10, with some Algerian newspapers putting the figure at up to 250.
About 60,000 people have died in the five-year-old conflict, which erupted in 1992 after the authorities cancelled a general election dominated by Islamists.

One eyewitness, describing Tuesday's ambush in the heart of Algiers, said: "They waited for him to reach the last step (of the stone staircase leading from the building) and before he could get into his armoured car they emptied at least one magazine into his body."
Benhamouda's bodyguard and a warden at the union building were also killed, witnesses said. The Algerian news agency APS said the bodyguard died and the other was wounded.

No group has claimed responsibility for the killing. But Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour said Benhamouda died in a "cowardly terrorist attack", using Algeria's official term for killings they blame on Moslem fundamentalists.
Benhamouda kept a relative social peace through his reign over the UGTA, enabling the government to carry out economic reforms and gain International Monetary Fund praise for its performance.
Victims of the violence in Algeria include President Mohamed Boudiaf, assassinated in June 1992 in the eastern town of Annaba, by a member of his own security force.

Many other senior government figures and leading personalities have died in the slaughter which recently has seen babies only months old killed by having their throats cut, and ordinary men and women beheaded.
